name: Learn: Debugging & Observability
objective: CKAD › Application Observability and Maintenance (15%). Goal: diagnose and fix failing workloads using kubectl logs, describe, and events — CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, Pending (unschedulable), reading container stdout, and a failing readiness probe.
description: The core CKAD debugging loop: read logs, describe, and events to find why a workload is unhealthy, then fix it. Covers CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, a Pending pod, retrieving a line from container logs, and a broken readiness probe.

questions.title: Fix a CrashLoopBackOff pod (read logs)
questions.teach: A pod in **CrashLoopBackOff** starts, its process exits, and Kubernetes keeps restarting it with a growing back-off (10s, 20s, 40s … capped at 5m). The state means *restarting repeatedly*, not a specific error — you must read logs to find the actual cause. **The debugging loop (in order):** - **`kubectl logs `** — stdout/stderr of the *current* container; usually names the cause. - **`kubectl logs --previous`** (`-p`) — the logs of the *last crashed* instance. Essential for CrashLoop, because the current container may have just restarted and its logs are empty or incomplete. - Multi-container pods: add **`-c `** (or `--all-containers`); default is the first container. - **`kubectl describe pod`** — Last State, **exit code** (0 = clean; 1/2 = app error; 137 = SIGKILL/OOMKilled; 143 = SIGTERM), Reason, and `Restart Count`. - **`kubectl get events`** / `kubectl get pod -o wide` for scheduling/node context. **Common crash causes:** wrong command/args (image has no such binary), a config/env it needs is missing, it does real work and exits 0 (a Job's job, not a long-lived pod), or **OOMKilled** (exit 137 — bump the memory limit). **Gotchas:** - You **can** change a pod's `image` in place (`kubectl set image pod/ =`), but **not** its `command`/`args` or most other fields — for those, delete and recreate (or edit the controller, not the pod). - `logs` with no `--previous` on a fast-crashing pod often shows nothing; reach for `-p`. - A `restartPolicy: Never` pod won't loop — it goes to `Error`/`Completed` and stays; CrashLoop needs `Always`/`OnFailure`. - `exit 0` is still a crash for a long-lived pod — Kubernetes restarts even on success under `Always`. Here a pod runs a command that errors out immediately. Read the logs, learn the cause, and replace it with a command that stays up.
questions.prompt:
Pod `crasher` in namespace `ckad-observability` is in CrashLoopBackOff — its command is wrong. Inspect it, then fix it so it runs a long-lived process (image `busybox:1.36`, e.g. `sleep 3600`).

Target: pod `crasher` is `Running` and `Ready` (recreate it — you can't patch a pod's command in place).
questions.hint: `kubectl logs crasher -n ckad-observability` (or `--previous`) shows the error. Delete and recreate: `kubectl delete pod crasher -n ckad-observability` then `kubectl run crasher -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600`.
questions.solution:
kubectl logs crasher -n ckad-observability --previous
kubectl describe pod crasher -n ckad-observability
kubectl delete pod crasher -n ckad-observability
kubectl run crasher -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod crasher -n ckad-observability   # Running, Ready

verification.description: pod 'crasher' is Running and Ready (no CrashLoop)

questions.title: Fix an ImagePullBackOff Deployment (describe + events)
questions.teach:
**ErrImagePull** (first failure) → **ImagePullBackOff** (kubelet retrying with back-off) means the node can't pull the image. **`kubectl logs` is useless** — the container never started — so you diagnose with **`kubectl describe pod`** and **`kubectl get events`**, whose Events section shows `Failed to pull image ...` with the *exact* reference tried and the underlying error.

**Common causes (read the event text):**
- Wrong **tag** — `manifest ... not found` / `not found: manifest unknown` (the step's case).
- Wrong **repo/name** or typo — `repository does not exist`.
- **Private registry, no credentials** — `pull access denied` / `unauthorized`. Fix: a `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` Secret referenced via `imagePullSecrets` on the pod spec (or the ServiceAccount).
- **Rate limited / network** to the registry.
- `:latest` with `imagePullPolicy: Always` can re-pull and surprise you; a pinned tag defaults to `IfNotPresent`.

**Fixing & gotchas:**
- You can't `kubectl set image` a bare pod's running container the way you edit a controller — but for a **Deployment** use `kubectl set image deploy/<name> <container>=<image>`, which triggers a rollout.
- `kubectl set image` needs the **container name** (not the pod name): `deploy/web web=...`. Get it from `kubectl describe` or the spec.
- Don't confuse `ImagePullBackOff` (can't fetch image) with `CrashLoopBackOff` (image ran then died) — different first tool (`describe`/`events` vs `logs`).
- A fix on the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet; watch `kubectl rollout status`.

A Deployment references a tag that doesn't exist. Find the bad image in the events, then set a valid one.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `web` in `ckad-observability` is stuck — its pods are in ImagePullBackOff because of a bad image tag. Diagnose with describe/events, then update it to a pullable image (`nginx:1.25-alpine`).

Target: Deployment `web` has its pods `Running` (all replicas available).
questions.hint: `kubectl describe deploy web -n ckad-observability` and `kubectl get events -n ckad-observability` show the failed image. Fix with `kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.25-alpine -n ckad-observability`.
questions.solution:
kubectl get pods -n ckad-observability
kubectl describe pod -l app=web -n ckad-observability | grep -A3 Events
kubectl set image deploy/web web=nginx:1.25-alpine -n ckad-observability
kubectl rollout status deploy/web -n ckad-observability

questions.title: Fix a Pending pod (unschedulable resources)
questions.teach:
A pod stays **Pending** when the scheduler can't bind it to any node. The reason is in **`kubectl describe pod`** → Events as a **`FailedScheduling`** message. Scheduling weighs **requests** (not limits): the scheduler sums each node's allocatable minus already-requested, and needs room for *this* pod's `resources.requests`.

**Common `FailedScheduling` reasons and their fixes:**
- **`Insufficient cpu` / `Insufficient memory`** — requests exceed any node's free allocatable (the step's case). Lower the request, or add capacity. CPU is `100m` = 0.1 core; memory suffixes `Mi`/`Gi`.
- **`node(s) had untolerated taint ...`** — add a matching **toleration** (effects `NoSchedule`/`PreferNoSchedule`/`NoExecute`), or remove the taint. The control-plane node is tainted `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`.
- **`didn't match node affinity/selector`** — your `nodeSelector`/`nodeAffinity` matches no node's labels.
- **`didn't match pod affinity/anti-affinity`** / topology-spread (`maxSkew`, `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule`) can't be satisfied.
- **Unbound PVC** — `pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims` (no PV/StorageClass to bind).
- **`too many pods`** — node pod cap reached.

**Gotchas:**
- Scheduling is about **requests**, not limits — a huge limit alone won't block scheduling; a huge request will.
- You can't patch a pod's `resources` in place — delete and recreate (or fix the controller template).
- `nodeName` set directly **bypasses the scheduler** entirely (no FailedScheduling event, but it can get stuck for other reasons).
- `limits` without `requests` → Kubernetes defaults requests to equal the limits, which can itself cause Pending.

Here a pod requests far more CPU than the cluster has. Diagnose it, then recreate it with a sane request so it schedules.
questions.prompt:
Pod `bigask` in `ckad-observability` is stuck `Pending` — it requests an impossible amount of CPU. Diagnose with describe, then recreate it (image `busybox:1.36`, `sleep 3600`) with a schedulable CPU request such as `100m`.

Target: pod `bigask` is `Running`.
questions.hint: `kubectl describe pod bigask -n ckad-observability` → Events show `FailedScheduling ... Insufficient cpu`. Delete it, then recreate with a small request, e.g. `kubectl run bigask -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"bigask","image":"busybox:1.36","command":["sleep","3600"],"resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m"}}}]}}'`.
questions.solution:
kubectl describe pod bigask -n ckad-observability | grep -A5 Events
kubectl delete pod bigask -n ckad-observability
kubectl run bigask -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"bigask","image":"busybox:1.36","command":["sleep","3600"],"resources":{"requests":{"cpu":"100m"}}}]}}'
kubectl get pod bigask -n ckad-observability   # Running

questions.title: Capture a line from container logs
questions.teach:
Observability isn't only about failures — you also read an app's stdout to confirm behaviour. **`kubectl logs`** returns whatever the container wrote to **stdout/stderr** (the container-logging contract; apps logging to a file inside the container won't show up).

**Useful `kubectl logs` flags:**
- `-f` follow (stream), `--tail=N` last N lines, `--since=10m` / `--since-time=`, `--timestamps`.
- `-p` / `--previous` — previous (crashed) instance.
- `-c <container>` / `--all-containers` for multi-container pods; `-l app=web` across pods by label; `kubectl logs deploy/<name>` picks one pod of a controller.

**ConfigMap creation — all the ways (symmetric with Secret; swap `create configmap`→`create secret generic` and `--from-literal`/`--from-file` stay the same):**
- `--from-literal=key=value` (the step's case; repeatable).
- `--from-file=./path` (filename → key, contents → value) or `--from-file=key=./path`.
- `--from-file=./dir/` (every file in the dir → a key).
- `--from-env-file=file.env` (each `K=V` line → a key).

**Consuming a ConfigMap later (exam staple — three methods):**
- Single-key env: `env[].valueFrom.configMapKeyRef` (Secret: `secretKeyRef`).
- Bulk env: `envFrom[].configMapRef` (Secret: `secretRef`).
- **Volume mount**: each key becomes a file; use `subPath` to mount a single key as one file.

**Gotchas:** env values are read **once at pod start** (change the ConfigMap → restart the pod), while **mounted** volumes update (with a delay); `immutable: true` locks a ConfigMap/Secret; missing keys fail the pod unless marked `optional: true`. Secret values are base64 in the API (not encryption).

Run a pod that prints a known token, read it back with `kubectl logs`, and prove you captured it by storing it in a ConfigMap.
questions.prompt:
Run a pod `logger` (image `busybox:1.36`) whose command prints the exact line `MARKER=ckad-obs-42` to stdout and then stays running (e.g. `echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600`). Read it back with `kubectl logs`, then create a ConfigMap `captured` in `ckad-observability` with key `token` set to that value `ckad-obs-42`.

Target: pod `logger` logged `MARKER=ckad-obs-42` AND ConfigMap `captured` has `token=ckad-obs-42`.
questions.hint: `kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'`, then `kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability`, then `kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run logger -n ckad-observability --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sh -c 'echo MARKER=ckad-obs-42; sleep 3600'
kubectl logs logger -n ckad-observability   # MARKER=ckad-obs-42
kubectl create configmap captured -n ckad-observability --from-literal=token=ckad-obs-42

verification.description: logger printed the marker AND configmap 'captured' holds token=ckad-obs-42

questions.title: Fix a failing readiness probe
questions.teach:
A **readiness probe** gates traffic: until it passes, the pod is `Running` but **not Ready**, so it's removed from Service **endpoints** and doesn't count toward a Deployment's `availableReplicas`. A probe pointed at the wrong path/port never succeeds, pinning availability at 0 even though the container is perfectly healthy. `kubectl describe pod` shows `Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 404`.

**The three probe types (same handlers, different reaction to failure):**
- **liveness** — on failure the kubelet **restarts** the container (fixes hangs). A bad liveness probe causes a restart loop.
- **readiness** — on failure the pod is pulled from **endpoints** (no restart); it recovers when it passes again.
- **startup** — gates liveness/readiness for **slow starters**; while it runs the others are suspended, so a slow boot isn't killed.

**Handlers (any probe):** `httpGet` (path/port/scheme/httpHeaders; 200–399 = success), `exec` (command; exit 0 = success), `tcpSocket` (port open), `grpc` (port/service).

**Timing fields:** `initialDelaySeconds`, `periodSeconds`, `timeoutSeconds`, `failureThreshold`, `successThreshold`.

**Gotchas:**
- `successThreshold` **must be 1 for liveness and startup**; readiness may be >1.
- A too-short `initialDelaySeconds`/`failureThreshold` on **liveness** kills apps mid-boot — prefer a **startup** probe for slow starts.
- `httpGet.port` is the **container** port (name or number), not a Service port; wrong path **or** port both yield failures.
- Probes run from the **kubelet on the node**, inside the pod's network namespace — not from your laptop.
- You can't patch a pod's probe in place; edit the **controller template** (`kubectl edit`/`patch deploy`) so the new ReplicaSet picks it up.

Here a Deployment's httpGet readiness path is wrong. Fix the path so the pods become Ready.
questions.prompt:
Deployment `ready-web` in `ckad-observability` runs nginx but stays at 0 available — its readiness probe does an httpGet on the wrong path `/healthz` (nginx returns 404). Fix the probe path to `/` so the pods pass readiness.

Target: Deployment `ready-web` reports `availableReplicas` ≥ 1.
questions.hint: `kubectl describe pod -l app=ready-web -n ckad-observability` shows the 404. Patch the path: `kubectl patch deploy ready-web -n ckad-observability --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/"}]'` (or `kubectl edit`).
questions.solution:
kubectl describe pod -l app=ready-web -n ckad-observability | grep -i readiness
kubectl patch deploy ready-web -n ckad-observability --type=json -p='[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/readinessProbe/httpGet/path","value":"/"}]'
kubectl rollout status deploy/ready-web -n ckad-observability
